title: Chilli heat
subtitle: Spice and wine
objectives: Explain the role of alcohol and tannin

steps.title: Heat and wine
steps.body: Chilli heat, from capsaicin, is not a taste but a feeling of burning. In the mouth it makes alcohol feel hotter, and it makes tannin and bitterness more aggressive. A high-alcohol, tannic red with a hot curry can feel like fire. The wine also loses fruit.

steps.title: Why sugar helps
steps.body: Sugar and low alcohol calm the burn. Capsaicin dissolves in alcohol and fat, so strong drinks spread it around the mouth. A touch of sweetness and moderate alcohol soothe instead. An off-dry Riesling at 9 or 10% alcohol is a classic match for spicy Thai or Sichuan food.
steps.highlight: Off-dry and low alcohol calm the heat

steps.prompt: Which wine is the best match for a hot Thai curry?
steps.explanation: Lower alcohol and a touch of sugar calm chilli heat. High alcohol and tannin make it burn more.

steps.title: Other good options
steps.body: Fruity, aromatic whites like Gewürztraminer handle spice well. Among reds, choose low-tannin, juicy wines served slightly cool, such as Beaujolais. Fruity rosé also works. Avoid big oak, high alcohol and firm tannin.
steps.highlight: Fruity, aromatic, low tannin, moderate alcohol

steps.prompt: Which features make a wine harder to pair with chilli?
steps.explanation: High alcohol, firm tannin and heavy oak all clash with heat. Sugar and lower alcohol help.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Chilli heat makes alcohol, tannin and bitterness feel stronger
Off-dry, lower-alcohol wines calm the burn
Choose fruity, aromatic, low-tannin wines with spicy food
